cls: Acridine antiprotozoal / antimalarial (historical); also immunomodulatory antimalarial-type agent
pharm: A tricyclic acridine that intercalates into DNA and disrupts replication and transcription; historically a systemic antimalarial, it is now used mainly for nitroimidazole-refractory giardiasis and as an adjunct in cutaneous lupus, and off-label as a pleurodesis sclerosant.

Take after meals with a full glass of water to reduce GI upset
Avoid; crosses the placenta with animal fetal-death data
Avoid if possible; small amounts appear in milk
Caution; extend dosing intervals to avoid accumulation
Caution with LFT monitoring; concentrates heavily in the liver
G6PD, LFTs, CBC, mental status; eye exam if used >6 months
summary: Mepacrine (quinacrine) is a synthetic acridine antiparasitic developed in the 1920s and used extensively as a WWII antimalarial before being superseded by chloroquine. It is no longer commercially manufactured or FDA-approved in the US and is obtained only through compounding pharmacies or overseas. Its principal modern use is second-line giardiasis (100 mg three times daily for 5-7 days) that has failed nitroimidazoles, and as an adjunct (usually 100 mg/day added to hydroxychloroquine) for treatment-resistant cutaneous and discoid lupus and related dermatologic disease. Historically it treated intestinal tapeworm and, by intrapleural instillation, served as a pleurodesis sclerosant. It acts largely by DNA intercalation, has extensive tissue distribution and a long half-life (about 5-14 days), and accumulates in liver, spleen, lung, and skin - producing a reversible yellow discoloration of skin, sclera, and secretions. Key toxicities include toxic psychosis, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, exacerbation of psoriasis or porphyria, hepatitis, and rare aplastic anemia, so careful monitoring is required.
indications: Cutaneous and discoid (chronic) lupus erythematosus, usually as an adjunct to hydroxychloroquine

dosage.n: Second-line after metronidazole or tinidazole; take after meals
Usually adjunct to hydroxychloroquine; keep <=100 mg/day

dosage.n: Given with sodium bicarbonate and antiemetic/purgative
Transient fever common; rapid pleural absorption

Warn the patient that yellow discoloration of skin, urine, sclera, and secretions is expected and harmless (not jaundice)
Pleurodesis is instilled by a clinician, not given orally
Because of the long half-life, steady state is reached only after about 4 weeks of continuous dosing
Screen for G6PD deficiency before starting
moa: Quinacrine is a tricyclic acridine structurally related to other antimalarials. Its principal molecular action is intercalation between adjacent DNA base pairs, unwinding the helix and inhibiting DNA and RNA replication, transcription, and translation. For antimalarial activity this DNA binding interferes with parasite replication and inhibits nucleotide incorporation into parasite nucleic acids; additional proposed acridine mechanisms include topoisomerase II inhibition, mitochondrial bc1-complex inhibition, inhibition of haemozoin formation, and phospholipase inhibition. In giardiasis and cestode infection it disrupts parasite metabolism and attachment. In lupus and inflammatory skin disease the effect is immunomodulatory and anti-inflammatory, through phospholipase A2 inhibition (reducing prostaglandin and leukotriene generation), ultraviolet-light absorption, and interference with antigen presentation and cytokine production. The mechanism of its idiosyncratic toxicities, such as hepatotoxicity, is unclear and may involve a reactive metabolite.

relative: Psoriasis (may precipitate a severe or exfoliative attack)
Concurrent primaquine or other hepatotoxic drugs
monitor: Skin (lichenoid reaction) and eyes (if used more than 6 months)

preg: Quinacrine crosses the placenta, and an animal intrauterine study showed increased fetal death; human data are lacking. It should not be used in pregnancy or by women planning pregnancy.
lact: Small amounts are excreted in milk. No adverse infant effects are formally reported, but data are limited, so avoid use during breastfeeding if possible.
renal: Reduced renal function may require longer dosing intervals to prevent accumulation, increased skin yellowing, and toxicity; use with caution.
hepatic: Quinacrine concentrates heavily in the liver (up to about 20,000 times plasma levels) and can cause dose-related hepatotoxicity and rare idiosyncratic hepatitis or acute liver failure. Monitor liver function; mixed-pattern enzyme elevations typically occur 1-6 weeks into therapy, are usually asymptomatic, and resolve 1-2 months after stopping.

major: Alcohol - disulfiram-like reaction (nausea, vomiting, flushing); avoid
Primaquine - quinacrine raises plasma primaquine levels and increases its toxicity; avoid concurrent use
moderate: Other hepatotoxic drugs - additive liver injury; monitor LFTs
Other 4-aminoquinolines (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine) - additive ocular, dermatologic, and hematologic toxicity even though used together in lupus
interactions.food: Take with or after food to reduce gastrointestinal upset.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - a disulfiram-like reaction can occur.
interactions.diagnostics: The vivid yellow discoloration of skin, urine, and secretions can be mistaken for jaundice on examination.

common: Yellow discoloration of skin, sclera, nails, urine, sweat, and tears (reversible, dose-dependent)
emergency: Aplastic anemia / severe cytopenia (bruising, bleeding, infection)

monitoring: Ophthalmologic examination if used more than 6 months
counsel: Expect temporary, harmless yellowing of your skin, eyes, and urine - this is not jaundice
Take after meals with a full glass of water
Avoid alcohol completely while taking this medicine
Report mood or behavior changes, hallucinations, an itchy rash, unusual bruising or bleeding, fever or infection, or yellow eyes with feeling unwell
Attend your blood-test and eye-exam appointments
Tell your doctor if you have G6PD deficiency, psoriasis, a psychiatric history, or liver or kidney disease
pk: Rapid oral absorption; clinical effect builds over days to weeks
Plasma peak about 2-12 hours after an oral dose
Steady state at about 4 weeks; effects persist days to weeks after stopping
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: NOT FDA-approved and not commercially manufactured in the US - available only via compounding or overseas (an FDA compounding safety notice exists)
The famous WWII frontline antimalarial 'Atabrine'; yellow pigmentation is NOT jaundice
In lupus it does not itself cause retinopathy, making it a useful add-on to hydroxychloroquine, but combination therapy still needs ocular monitoring
Keep the lupus dose around 100 mg/day - aplastic anemia is linked to higher doses
A lichenoid eruption is a red flag that can precede aplastic anemia - stop the drug and check the CBC
missed: Take a missed dose when you remember; if it is near the next dose, skip it (the very long half-life limits the impact of a single missed dose). Do not take a double dose.
overdose: There is no specific antidote and management is supportive. Overdose amplifies the drug's toxicities - CNS stimulation and toxic psychosis, seizures, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal effects, and hematologic and hepatic toxicity. Provide supportive care, seizure control, and cardiac and CNS monitoring, and consult poison control.
